tool.name: RAVGBurnSeverity

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/data-tools/ravg-burn-severity.html
Finds fires mapped by Rapid Assessment of Vegetation Condition after Wildfire (RAVG), a program of the USDA Forest Service, by name, year and place, and writes their perimeters. For each fire it can fetch the classified rasters of percent basal area loss, percent canopy cover loss and the composite burn index, with every class named, and it can ask the Burn Severity Portal to email a link to the fire's data bundle, which holds the continuous values. RAVG maps fires that burn at least 1,000 acres of forested National Forest System land. United States only. Works at every license level.

tool.usage:
What RAVG maps. RAVG estimates what a fire did to the trees. Like MTBS it starts from the Normalized Burn Ratio of an image taken before the fire and one taken after it. It then uses the Relative differenced Normalized Burn Ratio, RdNBR, which divides the change (dNBR) by the square root of the pre-fire NBR, so that a stand with little vegetation to lose and a dense stand are measured on the same footing (Miller and Thode 2007). Regression equations, built from field plots where the loss was measured on the ground, turn the index into three estimates: the percent of basal area lost, the percent of canopy cover lost, and the composite burn index (CBI), a field score of fire effects from 0 to 3.
The classes are fixed. Unlike MTBS, RAVG's classes are the same in every fire. Basal area loss has seven classes (0%; more than 0% to less than 10%; 10% to less than 25%; 25% to less than 50%; 50% to less than 75%; 75% to less than 90%; 90% to 100%), canopy cover loss has five (0%; more than 0% to less than 25%; 25% to less than 50%; 50% to less than 75%; 75% to 100%), and the composite burn index has four (unchanged, 0 to less than 0.1; low, 0.1 to less than 1.25; moderate, 1.25 to less than 2.25; high, 2.25 to 3.0).
Its limits. RAVG is made for the Forest Service's reforestation planning, about 45 days after a fire is contained, for fires that burn at least 1,000 acres of forested National Forest System land (500 acres in the Eastern and Southern regions since 2016). Its equations are calibrated for forest. In vegetation that is not forest the numbers do not mean what they say.
United States only. This is a program of the United States Government. It maps fires in the United States and its territories, and nowhere else.
Finding fires. Give any of a fire name, a range of years, a study area and the programs' fire IDs; a fire must match all that you give. The study area only selects fires: every fire whose perimeter touches it is written whole, including the parts outside it. Nothing is clipped.
The classified rasters are copies. The rasters this tool fetches come from public map services, which hold copies of the program's national mosaics in the Web Mercator coordinate system. They are right for looking and for overlay. Their cells are not 30 meters on the ground, so do not count cells to measure area. Each raster's attribute table names every class (Class_Name) and gives its true area (Hectares, Acres) and its share of the fire (Percent). Cells the program could not assess, such as cloud, are named as a mask class and left out of the percentages. The original cells, in the fire's own projection, are in the fire's data bundle.
Which fires have a raster. The map service carries RAVG's yearly mosaics for 2012 to 2023 only. The catalog lists RAVG fires from other years as well; their rasters are in their data bundles.
Data bundles come by email. A fire's data bundle holds what the map services do not: the continuous indices, in the fire's own projection with true 30-meter cells, and the rasters of fires too recent to be in the national mosaics. The Burn Severity Portal does not hand bundles to a program. Give an email address and this tool asks the portal for the bundles of every fire it found, in one request of up to 500 fires. Nothing is downloaded by the tool. The portal sends an email with a link, usually within minutes; you download the zip file yourself (the link works for 30 days), and then run the Load Burn Severity Bundle tool on it.
The internet. The tool reads the fire catalog of the Burn Severity Portal and the map services of the U.S. Geological Survey and the USDA Forest Service. If one of them cannot be reached, the tool stops with a message that names it, and writes nothing.

param.name: fire_name
param.displayname: Fire name (all or part of it; several separated by semicolons)

dialogReference.para: All or part of a fire's name, in capitals or not: museum finds MUSEUM. Several names can be given, separated by semicolons, and a fire matching any of them is found. Many fires share a name, so give years or a study area as well. Empty for any name.
The first year of ignition to include, from 1984. Empty for no limit.
The last year of ignition to include. Empty for no limit. For one year, give the same year in both boxes.

A year later than the current one is accepted, so 9999 means "through the latest fires". The tool then asks for fires through the current year, and its messages name the years that were not available.

A polygon layer or feature class. Selected polygons are used when there is a selection, and a definition query is honored. Every fire whose perimeter touches a polygon is found and written whole: the study area selects fires and does not clip them.

param.name: extent
param.displayname: Or a rectangle as the study area

dialogReference.para: A rectangle, in any coordinate system. Every fire whose perimeter touches it is found and written whole. Give a study area layer or a rectangle, not both.

param.name: fire_ids
param.displayname: Fire IDs (the programs' event identifiers, separated by semicolons)

dialogReference.para: The identifiers the programs give fires, such as AZ3525811164320190721 (the state, the latitude and longitude of the fire's center, and the ignition date). They are in the fire_id field of this tool's output, and the same fire has the same identifier in MTBS, RAVG and BAER. Use them to ask for exactly the fires you mean.

An identifier stands for every assessment of the fire. A fire can have more than one: an initial and an extended assessment, for example. To ask for one of them only, add a colon and that assessment's map ID (the map_id field of this tool's output), as in AZ3525811164320190721:10016328.

param.name: out_perimeters
param.displayname: Output fire perimeters (in a file geodatabase)

dialogReference.para: The polygon feature class to create, directly inside a file geodatabase, with one perimeter for each fire found and the fire's name, identifier, ignition date, type, acres and the thresholds its analyst set. An existing feature class of that name is replaced.

param.name: products
param.displayname: Classified rasters to fetch for each fire

dialogReference.para: The classified rasters to fetch for each fire: percent basal area loss in seven classes, percent canopy cover loss in five, and the composite burn index in four. Each is cut to the fire's perimeter and its attribute table names each class. Uncheck everything to write the perimeters alone.

param.name: raster_workspace
param.displayname: Folder or file geodatabase for the rasters (empty: the geodatabase of the perimeters)

dialogReference.para: Where the classified rasters are written: a folder (GeoTIFF files) or a file geodatabase. Left empty, they go into the geodatabase of the output perimeters. Each raster is named for its program, fire, year and product, and a raster of the same name is replaced.

param.name: bundle_email
param.displayname: Email address for a request of the fires' data bundles (empty: no request)

dialogReference.para: An email address. When one is given, the tool asks the Burn Severity Portal to prepare the data bundles of every fire it found and to send a download link to this address. Nothing is downloaded by the tool: you open the email, download the zip file yourself, and run the Load Burn Severity Bundle tool on it. The address is sent to the portal and is not kept anywhere by this tool. Empty for no request.

param.name: bundle_images
param.displayname: Include the pre-fire and post-fire images in the bundles

dialogReference.para: Checked, the bundle request also asks for the two satellite images each assessment was made from: the reflectance image taken before the fire and the one taken after it. They make the zip file much larger. Unchecked, the bundle holds the perimeter, the classified rasters and the continuous indices only. Used only when an email address is given.

The coordinate system the portal writes the bundle's rasters in. UTM is the zone of each fire, with true 30-meter cells, and suits work on one fire or one region. Albers is the single equal-area projection of the national mosaics, and suits work on fires spread across the country, because every fire is then on the same grid. Used only when an email address is given.
The number of fires that matched.
The classified rasters that were fetched.

scriptExample.title: RAVG Burn Severity example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: The perimeter of the 2021 Telegraph Fire and its three classified rasters.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path arcpy.jenness.RAVGBurnSeverity( fire_name="telegraph", year_from=2021, year_to=2021, out_perimeters=r"D:\data\fire.gdb\Telegraph_RAVG"))

scriptExample.title: Basal area loss only, into a folder
scriptExample.para: One product, written as GeoTIFF files in a folder.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path arcpy.jenness.RAVGBurnSeverity( fire_name="museum", year_from=2019, year_to=2019, out_perimeters=r"D:\data\fire.gdb\Museum_RAVG", products="'Basal area loss (7 classes)'", raster_workspace=r"D:\data\ravg_rasters"))
